extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of moral philosophy; academic readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the foundations of ethics arguing that compassion is the innate moral incentive and that moral character is essentially innate and largely unteachable; explores conscience, moral responsibility, and the need for metaphysical grounding. Targeted as a theoretical, academic treatment of ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as an implanted natural principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another principle which Hobbes did not perceive at all. It was implanted in man in order to soften, in certain circumstances, the fierceness of his self-love, and it moderates the ardour, which he feels for his own well-being, by producing a certain innate aversion to the sight of a fellow-creature's suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compassion is presented as an innate faculty that restrains self-love and provides the psychological basis for moral behaviour; it is contrasted with Hobbes' account and described as 'the only natural virtue' that even scepticism must recognise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as source of social virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: From this one quality spring all the social virtues ... what is generosity, clemency, humanity, if not compassion, applied to the weak, to the guilty, or to the human race, as a whole? Even benevolence and friendship ... are seen to result from a constant compassion, directed upon a particular object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats compassion as the origin of generosity, clemency, humanity, benevolence, and friendship, arguing that these virtues are applications or specialisations of compassion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification with the sufferer as mechanism of pity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more closely the living spectator identifies himself with the living sufferer, the more active does pity become. In fact, how is it that we let ourselves be moved to pity, if not by getting out of our own consciousness, and becoming identified with the living sufferer?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pity arises by imaginatively entering another's experience; cultivating objects on which 'the expansive force of [one's] heart can act' enlarges one's nature and predisposes one to pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as social regulator in the state of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: This it is, which in the state of nature, takes the place of laws, customs, and virtues ... which will restrain every able-bodied savage ... from robbing a weak child, or depriving an infirm old man of the subsistence won by hard toil; ... inspires all men ... with another rule of natural goodness ... 'Do what is good for yourself with the least possible harm to others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compassion functions like an internal social law that discourages harming the vulnerable and recommends minimizing harm to others while pursuing one's own good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference of character is innate and ineradicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference of character is innate, and ineradicable. The wicked man is born with his wickedness ... nor can the former change his nature a whit more than the latter. ... All virtue arising from premeditation is not worth much. What is wanted is feeling or habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues against the idea that virtue can be taught into being; character dispositions (good or bad) are presented as original, fixed, and not fundamentally alterable by instruction alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian empirical vs intelligible character distinction (permanence of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant ... showed that the empirical character, which manifests itself in time and in multiplicity of action, is a phaenomenon; while the reality behind it is the intelligible character, which, being the essential constitution of the Thing in itself underlying the phaenomenon, is independent of time, space, plurality, and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metaphysical distinction is used to explain why character remains fixed and why outward actions may vary while the underlying 'what one is' remains constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental springs of human action: Egoism, Malice, Compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: The three fundamental springs of human action--Egoism, Malice, Compassion--are inherent in every one in different and strangely unequal proportions. Their combination in any given case determines the weight of the motives that present themselves, and shapes the resulting line of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral behaviour is analysed as the outcome of differing innate susceptibilities to these three motives; different natures respond only to the stimuli they are sensitive to (analogy to chemical reactivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness of heart defined as all-embracing compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness of heart consists of a deeply felt, all-embracing Compassion for everything that has breath, and especially for man; ... this goodness of heart, in the first place restrains a man from doing any sort of harm to others, and, next, it bids him give succour whenever and wherever he sees distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness implies both the avoidance of harm and active help; in extreme cases it can lead to self-effacement or sacrifice for many others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of moral education: intellect vs will
rubrics_metrics.description: By the proper presentment of motives legality may be secured, but not morality. ... It is possible to remodel what one does, but not what one wills to do; and it is to the will alone that real moral worth belongs. Instruction may alter the selection of means, but not the choice of the ultimate object which the individual keeps before him ... this is determined by his will in accordance with its original nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction can clarify judgment and change behaviour (means), but cannot alter the innate will or ultimate ends; penitentiary systems that educate the 'head' aim to change behaviour, not the 'heart.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as register of acts revealing changeless character
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience is that register of our acts, which is always growing longer, and therefore that acquaintance with ourselves which every day becomes more complete. Conscience concerns itself directly with all that we do; when, at one time, actuated by Egoism ... we turn a deaf ear to Compassion ... or ... we overcome ... and listen to the voice of the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conscience functions retrospectively: our acts accumulate as evidence of what we are, and conscience translates that empirical record into praise, blame, remorse, or satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blame and merit ultimately attributed to what one is (Operari sequitur esse)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is to this Esse, to what we are, that blame and merit must ultimately be attributed. ... For what we do is the only indisputable index of what we are, and reflects our character just as faithfully as symptoms betray the malady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral responsibility rests on character: acts reveal character, and therefore moral praise or blame is properly directed at the enduring nature (esse) rather than merely transient actions (operari).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics requires a metaphysical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The want is felt of a final interpretation (which, obviously, cannot but be metaphysical) of the ultimate data ... In Moral Science the need of a metaphysical basis is more urgent than in any other, because all systems ... attach to conduct not only an ethical, but also a metaphysical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond empirical grounding (compassion as fact), the author argues that a metaphysical account is necessary to fully explain the ethical phenomenon and its relation to human destiny; religion leverages this connection between metaphysics and ethics.
